concepts.title: Unit Testing with describe/it/expect
concepts.description: A test framework like Jest gives structure (describe/it) and a fluent assertion library (expect) to what would otherwise be ad-hoc scripts full of console.log and manual comparisons. Understanding how a test fails, and why isolated, repeatable unit tests matter, is the foundation the rest of testing builds on.
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose of describe and it (or test) blocks and how they organize related assertions into readable, isolated units.
Write assertions with expect using matchers like toBe, toEqual, toThrow, and toHaveLength, and explain when toBe is wrong and toEqual is required.
Explain what makes a test 'unit' rather than 'integration' -- isolating the function under test from its collaborators.
Use beforeEach/afterEach to reset shared state between tests and explain why leaking state across tests produces order-dependent failures.
Predict whether a given assertion passes or fails, and explain the specific mismatch a failing assertion reports.

sections.heading: Why Not Just console.log Everything?
describe and it: Organizing Related Assertions
expect and Matchers: toBe vs toEqual, and the Rest
sections.body:
expect(value) returns an object with chainable matcher methods describing what you expect to be true about value. The two most common, and the two people mix up most, are toBe and toEqual. **toBe** uses Object.is equality, which behaves like === for practical purposes. That's right for primitives (numbers, strings, booleans) but wrong for objects and arrays, because two different array instances with identical contents are never === each other. **toEqual** performs a recursive, structural (deep) comparison: every key and value inside an object or array must match, whether or not the two are the same object in memory. (toStrictEqual is the stricter variant: it also fails on properties that are explicitly undefined and on objects of different classes.)

```javascript
expect(2 + 2).toBe(4);                       // correct: primitives compare by value with toBe
expect({ id: 1 }).toEqual({ id: 1 });         // correct: toEqual compares structure
expect({ id: 1 }).toBe({ id: 1});             // FAILS: two different object instances, never ===
```

Other matchers to know from the start: toThrow(message) asserts that a function call throws (pass a function, expect(() => risky()).toThrow(), not expect(risky()).toThrow(), since the latter calls risky() immediately, outside Jest's control, before expect can catch anything; a string argument checks that the error message contains that text). toHaveLength(n) checks an array's or string's .length. toContain(item) checks array membership or substring presence. toBeNull, toBeUndefined, and toBeDefined check for those exact values, which matters because == would treat null and undefined as interchangeable. Prefixing any matcher with .not (expect(x).not.toBe(y)) inverts it. Choosing the matcher that matches your intent, with structural vs reference equality the most common mistake, is what makes a test useful rather than a false sense of security.

examples.title: A Small Module and Its Full Test Suite
examples.explanation: Each it block tests one behavior of slugify, phrased as a sentence describing what should be true. When 'collapses multiple internal spaces into one hyphen' fails, the name alone tells you which behavior regressed, before you read the assertion. All three tests use toBe rather than toEqual because slugify returns a primitive string, where reference and value equality coincide; toEqual would also work, but toBe signals to a reader that a primitive comparison is intended.

examples.title: toBe vs toEqual in Practice
examples.explanation: The commented-out toBe line would fail every time, however correct createUser is, because user and the literal passed to toBe are two distinct objects in memory, and === is false for any two separately created objects even with identical contents. toEqual walks both objects recursively, comparing keys and values (including nested arrays, like roles), and judges them equal by structure rather than identity, which is what you want to verify: not that it's the same object, but that its shape and values are correct.

misconceptions.description: toBe and toEqual are interchangeable -- they're just two names for 'check that this value is what I expected.'
misconceptions.clarification: toBe checks strict reference/primitive equality (like ===), while toEqual performs a recursive structural comparison of an object or array's contents. For primitives (numbers, strings, booleans) they behave identically, which is why the distinction goes unnoticed until someone uses toBe on an object or array and gets a confusing failure: the expected and received values look identical in the output (Jest even notes that the received value 'serializes to the same string'), because their contents are equal and only the object identity differs. The rule of thumb: use toBe for primitives, toEqual for objects and arrays.
misconceptions.fact: toBe checks strict reference/primitive equality (like ===), while toEqual performs a recursive structural comparison of an object or array's contents.

misconceptions.description: If a test's assertions are wrapped in a describe block, describe itself needs to catch failures, or a failing assertion will crash the whole test file and prevent any other tests from running.
misconceptions.clarification: describe is organizational: it groups related it blocks for readable output, while each it/test block is isolated by the test runner itself. A failing expect (or a thrown error) inside one it block is caught by Jest, that test is marked failed, and Jest runs every other it block in the file and in every other describe block unaffected. describe's presence or absence doesn't change this; the isolation is at the level of individual test blocks.
misconceptions.fact: describe is purely organizational -- it groups related it blocks for readable output, but each individual it/test block is independently isolated by the test runner itself.

exercises.prompt: Given this test file, which of the three tests pass and which fail when the suite runs? Explain the failure(s).
hints: The first test compares a primitive number with toBe. Is that the right matcher for a primitive?
The second test compares two objects with toBe. Are makeConfig()'s returned object and the literal passed to toBe ever the SAME object in memory, whatever properties they share?
toEqual, unlike toBe, compares objects by walking their structure recursively instead of checking whether they're the identical reference.
exercises.expectedAnswer: Test 1 passes (retries is a primitive number, and 3 === 3 is true). Test 2 FAILS (toBe on two separately created objects is always false whatever their contents, because they're different references). Test 3 passes (toEqual compares structure, and both objects have identical keys and values).
exercises.solutionExplanation: makeConfig().retries evaluates to the primitive number 3, and toBe on primitives is equivalent to ===, so 3 === 3 is true and test 1 passes. Test 2 calls makeConfig() (returning a new object) and compares it with toBe against a separate object literal. Both have identical keys and values, but they are two distinct objects in memory, and toBe's reference-equality check (like Object.is) treats any two distinct objects as unequal whatever their contents, so this test fails. Test 3 uses toEqual, which recursively compares structure (keys and values) rather than identity, and since both objects have retries: 3 and timeout: 1000, it passes.

exercises.prompt: Each of these two tests passes when run on its own, but when the whole file runs, the second one fails (and if the tests were in the other order, a different one would). Find the bug and fix it so both tests pass regardless of order.
hints: inventory is declared once, outside both it blocks. Is it reset anywhere between tests, or is the same array reused and mutated across both?
The first test pushes an item onto inventory and never removes it. If that test runs before the second one, what does the second test's inventory contain?
Use beforeEach to reset inventory to a fresh empty array before every test, rather than relying on the order tests run in.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original inventory array is created once, outside both tests, and the first test mutates it with .push('widget') without resetting it. Jest runs the tests in the order they're written, so 'adds an item' runs before 'starts empty for a fresh check', the second test inherits an inventory that already has one item, and toHaveLength(0) fails. (Reverse the order and the failure would move to the other test, which is how you can tell it's shared state rather than a wrong assertion.) The fix adds a beforeEach hook that reassigns inventory to a new empty array before every test, independent of execution order, so each test starts with an empty inventory and 'adds an item' can't leak into another test's starting state.

assessments.prompt: Why does `expect(getUser()).toBe({ id: 1, name: 'Amy' })` fail even when getUser() genuinely returns an object with exactly those values?
options: toBe only works on primitive values, so using it on any object always throws a TypeError.
toBe requires the expected value to be passed as a string, not an object literal.
The test is missing an await before getUser(), so it's comparing a Promise to an object.
toBe checks strict reference equality, and two separately created objects are never the same reference.
assessments.explanation: toBe implements strict equality (comparable to ===/Object.is), which for objects and arrays means 'is this the same object in memory,' not 'do these objects have matching contents.' getUser() returns a freshly created object, and the object literal in the test is a second, separate object, so they can never be === each other however identical their keys and values. toEqual is designed for this case: it compares structure recursively instead of checking identity. The “toBe only works on primitive values…” option is wrong: toBe doesn't throw on objects, it evaluates to false. The “The test is missing an await before…” option is a red herring with no basis in the code. The “toBe requires the expected value…” option is false: toBe accepts any value type, including object literals; it performs the wrong kind of comparison for this use case.

assessments.prompt: A test suite has ten `it` blocks inside one `describe` block. The third `it` block throws an uncaught error partway through. What happens to the other nine?
options: All ten tests inside that same describe block are marked failed as a group, though tests in other, separate describe blocks still run normally.

Jest catches the failure within that one it block, marks only that specific test as failed, and continues running every other it block in the file and in any other describe blocks, completely unaffected.
The remaining tests are skipped entirely and reported as 'pending' rather than actually run or evaluated at all.

The whole file stops running immediately -- none of the remaining it blocks execute at all, exactly like an uncaught exception would halt a plain script, and the remaining results are reported as unknown.
assessments.explanation: Each it block is isolated by the test runner: a thrown error or failed expect inside one it block is caught by Jest, that one test is marked failed, and Jest runs every other it block regardless of describe grouping. That's the opposite of a plain script of sequential code, where an uncaught exception stops everything after it. The “The whole file stops running immediately…” option describes plain-script behavior, not Jest's. The “All ten tests inside that same describe…” option assumes failures cascade to sibling tests, which they don't. The “The remaining tests are skipped entirely…” option invents a 'pending' state that doesn't apply: the other nine tests run and are evaluated normally.

assessments.prompt: Which of these correctly asserts that calling riskyFunction() throws an error, using Jest's toThrow matcher?
options: expect(() => riskyFunction()).toThrow('some message');
expect(riskyFunction).toBe(Error);
expect(riskyFunction()).toEqual(new Error('some message'));
expect(riskyFunction()).toThrow('some message');
assessments.explanation: toThrow has to be the one that calls the function, inside Jest's own try/catch machinery, so it can observe the throw, which means you pass a function (here wrapped in an arrow function) rather than the already computed result of calling it. The “expect(riskyFunction()).toThrow('some message');” option calls riskyFunction() immediately, while building the expect(...) argument, before the matcher is involved, so a throw there escapes as an uncaught error in the test instead of being asserted on. The “expect(riskyFunction).toBe(Error);” option compares the function itself to the Error constructor, which is unrelated to whether it throws. The “expect(riskyFunction()).toEqual(new Error('some message'));” option has the same problem as the “expect(riskyFunction()).toThrow('some message');” option (calling the function immediately) and uses the wrong matcher for a thrown value.

assessments.prompt: A test suite needs (1) an expensive, read-only setup step -- opening one shared database connection used, unmodified, by every test -- and (2) a plain in-memory array reset to empty before every individual test. Which combination of Jest hooks fits each need, respectively?
options: afterAll for the shared connection, afterEach for resetting the array.
describe for the connection, it for the array reset.

beforeAll for the shared, expensive, read-only connection, since it only needs to run once for the whole suite; beforeEach for resetting the mutable array, since it needs a guaranteed-fresh value before every single test.

beforeEach for both, since beforeEach is always the strictly safer choice regardless of what's actually being set up, and the cost of reconnecting for each test is negligible because Jest reuses the same connection behind the scenes.
assessments.explanation: beforeAll runs once per describe block, which suits expensive setup that's safe to share, read-only, across tests; redoing it before every test would waste time. beforeEach runs before every test, which is what a mutated shared array needs to stay independent between tests; reusing the array without resetting it would leak one test's changes into the next. The “afterAll for the shared connection, afterEach…” option puts the setup in the wrong lifecycle stage (after, not before). The “beforeEach for both, since beforeEach is always…” option ignores that beforeEach would pointlessly repeat the expensive setup for the read-only connection. The “describe for the connection, it for the array reset” option confuses hooks with structural blocks: describe and it aren't setup/teardown hooks.

assessments.prompt: Explain why tests should be independent of execution order, and how beforeEach helps enforce that -- use a concrete example of what goes wrong when tests silently share mutable state.
assessments.modelAnswer: A test suite's value comes from each test reporting pass or fail based only on the correctness of the code it exercises, not on which other tests ran earlier, in what order, or whether they ran at all (a runner can filter to a single test, randomize order, or spread test files across parallel workers). Once a piece of mutable state (a variable, an array, an object) is declared once and shared across several it blocks without a reset, tests stop being independent: one test's side effects (pushing to an array, incrementing a counter, writing to a shared object) become an invisible input to whatever test runs next. That's a maddening bug to debug, because the file read top to bottom looks correct and may even pass consistently in its normal order. The failure appears only when tests are reordered or filtered, which makes it look as if the runner is flaky rather than the tests having a hidden dependency. beforeEach solves this by running a setup function before every it block in its scope, so each test starts from the same known baseline whatever any earlier test did to that variable. Reassigning a shared array to a new empty array inside beforeEach (clearing it with .length = 0 also works) means a test that pushes an item and asserts a length of 1 can never cause a later, unrelated test to see that leftover item. Each test effectively gets a private copy of the fixture even though the variable name is shared across the file.

concepts.title: Mocking Modules and Dependencies
concepts.description: Real code depends on things you don't want a unit test near: a live database, a third-party payment API, the current wall-clock time. Mocking swaps those dependencies for fake, controllable stand-ins so a test can exercise your own logic in isolation, deterministically, without side effects or network calls.
learningObjectives: Explain why a unit test should not make real network calls, hit a real database, or depend on the current time, and what problems each of those causes in a test suite.
Create a mock function with jest.fn(), configure its return value, and assert on how it was called using toHaveBeenCalledWith.
Use jest.mock() to replace an entire module (e.g. a database client or an HTTP client) with a mocked version inside a test file.
Distinguish a mock (a fake with assertions about how it was called) from a stub (a fake that just returns canned data) conceptually, even though libraries blur the line.
Identify when mocking has gone too far -- a test so heavily mocked it no longer verifies real behavior -- and explain the resulting false sense of security.

sections.heading: Why Real Dependencies Don't Belong in a Unit Test
sections.body:
Consider a function that charges a credit card through a real payment provider's API, or one that looks up a user in a real database. Testing either against the real dependency has practical problems, not just 'purity' concerns. It's **slow**: a network round trip is milliseconds to seconds, and hundreds of tests making real calls make a suite nobody wants to run before every commit. It's **flaky**: a real service can be down, rate-limited, or slow for reasons unrelated to your code, and a test that sometimes fails for unrelated reasons trains everyone to ignore failures, which is worse than having no test. It's **expensive or dangerous**: you don't want a suite that charges a real card or sends a real email every time CI runs. And it's **hard to control**: testing 'what happens when the payment API returns a decline' or 'when the database connection times out' against a real service means forcing those conditions on demand, often impractical.

Mocking addresses all four: replace the real dependency with an in-memory stand-in that you control, that returns instantly, and that can be configured to simulate any scenario (success, failure, a specific edge case) the same way on every run.

sections.heading: jest.fn(): A Mock Function You Can Inspect
jest.mock(): Replacing an Entire Module
Mocks vs Stubs, and When You've Mocked Too Much
sections.body:
The testing literature distinguishes a **stub** (a fake that returns canned data when called, with no assertions about how it was called) from a **mock** in the strict sense (a fake you also make assertions against: toHaveBeenCalledWith, toHaveBeenCalledTimes). In practice, especially in the Jest ecosystem, both are called 'mocks,' and jest.fn() can serve as either: a stub if you only care about its configured return value, a strict mock if you also assert on the calls made to it. The distinction matters more conceptually than for choosing a Jest API.

What matters more in practice is not over-mocking. If a test mocks so much that what's left exercised is one trivial line of glue code, it can pass with full confidence while the integration between the pieces, the part most likely to have a bug, is never verified. A classic version: mocking db.getUser to return exactly the shape getUserDisplayName expects, without ever checking that the real database client returns data in that shape. If the real client's response format changes, or never matched the assumption, every one of these tests keeps passing and the bug ships undetected: false confidence. That's why unit tests with mocked boundaries are usually paired with integration tests (the next concept) that exercise at least one path through the real boundary, catching the class of bug that heavy mocking cannot.

examples.title: A Mock Function Standing In for a Callback
examples.explanation: processOrder's contract includes calling onComplete as a side effect, separate from its return value, so a plain expect on the return value wouldn't verify the callback contract. jest.fn() gives a fake onComplete with no real behavior, but Jest records the arguments of every call, which toHaveBeenCalledWith(35) checks. toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1) guards against a different bug: onComplete being called correctly but also called an extra, unwanted second time elsewhere in the function, which a check on arguments alone wouldn't catch.

examples.title: Mocking a Module Boundary with jest.mock
examples.explanation: jest.mock('./paymentGateway') intercepts every require of that module in this test file and replaces its exports with auto-mocked jest.fn() stand-ins, so no network call to a payment provider happens however often the test runs. mockResolvedValue({ status: 'declined' }) sets up a scenario that would be awkward to trigger on demand against a real gateway: a decline. expect(...).rejects.toThrow(...) asserts that an async function's returned Promise rejects with a matching error, which is what completeCheckout should do when it sees a non-approved status. The test verifies completeCheckout's real branching logic while the payment gateway stays faked.

misconceptions.description: Mocking a dependency means you're testing something fake, so a passing test with mocks doesn't really prove anything about your code.
misconceptions.clarification: A mock replaces the dependency, not the code under test. The logic inside the function you're testing (branching, calculations, error handling) still runs and is exercised; only the boundary (a database call, an API request) is faked so you control what it returns. What a heavily mocked test does NOT prove is that the real dependency behaves the way your mock assumed. That's a valid limitation, and it's why unit tests with mocked boundaries are complemented by integration tests that exercise at least one path through the real thing, not a reason to dismiss mocking as testing 'nothing real.'

misconceptions.description: jest.mock('./db') only affects the specific require('./db') call written in the same test file -- code inside other files that also require './db' still gets the real module.
misconceptions.clarification: jest.mock('./db') replaces that module for all code loaded within that test file's module resolution, including modules required by the file under test. If userService.js requires ./db internally, and the test file mocks ./db and then requires userService.js, userService.js's own require('./db') resolves to the SAME mocked version. That's what lets you test userService's logic while faking its internal database dependency, without userService.js knowing it's under test.

exercises.prompt: What does this test suite report -- does each test pass or fail, and why?
hints: notifyUser calls sendFn twice in its body. Read the function definition, not just the test names.
toHaveBeenCalledWith only checks that AT LEAST ONE call matched those arguments; it doesn't care how many calls were made in total.
toHaveBeenCalledTimes checks an exact count. If notifyUser calls sendFn twice, what does asserting toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1) actually check against?
exercises.expectedAnswer: The first test PASSES (sendFn was called with (42, 'Hello'), twice in fact, but toHaveBeenCalledWith only requires at least one matching call). The second test FAILS, because sendFn was called twice, not once: notifyUser calls sendFn(userId, message) two separate times.
exercises.solutionExplanation: notifyUser's body calls sendFn(userId, message) twice in a row. That's presumably a bug in notifyUser (it should notify once), but the question here is what the tests report. The first test's toHaveBeenCalledWith(42, 'Hello') passes because Jest checks whether ANY recorded call matched those arguments, and both did, so the duplicate doesn't matter. The second test's toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1) checks the exact call count, which is 2, so it fails and surfaces the double-call bug that the first test's matcher was never designed to catch.

exercises.prompt: This test is meant to verify that getUserDisplayName falls back to 'Unknown User' when the mocked database returns null, but it fails with 'TypeError: db.getUser.mockResolvedValue is not a function'. Find and fix the bug.
hints: db.getUser.mockResolvedValue(...) assumes db.getUser is already a jest mock function. Is it? Where is jest.mock('./db') called in this file?
Without jest.mock('./db'), require('./db') returns the REAL module, whose getUser is a plain function with no .mockResolvedValue method.

jest.mock() calls are typically placed near the top of the test file, before the mocked module is required, so this test file's own require AND userService.js's internal require both resolve to the mocked version.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original test file never calls jest.mock('./db'), so require('./db') returns the real db module, whose getUser is an ordinary function, not a jest.fn(), with no .mockResolvedValue method. Calling db.getUser.mockResolvedValue(null) on it throws 'TypeError: db.getUser.mockResolvedValue is not a function' before the test ever reaches getUserDisplayName. Adding jest.mock('./db') tells Jest to auto-mock the db module for this file, turning db.getUser into a jest.fn() with a working .mockResolvedValue. Because userService.js's own require('./db') resolves to that same mocked module, getUserDisplayName's await db.getUser(id) receives the configured null.

assessments.prompt: A test suite for a checkout function mocks the payment gateway, the email service, and the database so thoroughly that the only code left actually running is a single if statement. All tests pass. What is the most accurate assessment of this test suite?
options: The tests are equivalent to integration tests, since they cover every dependency the function uses.
The tests are excellent, since fully isolating the unit under test from every dependency is always the goal of unit testing.
Mocking three dependencies in one test file is invalid -- Jest only supports mocking a single module per test file.

The tests may give false confidence -- if so little of the checkout function's real logic and none of its real dependency behavior is being exercised, the tests mostly confirm the mocks return what they were told to return, not that the system works correctly end to end.
assessments.explanation: Mocking isolates the code under test from dependencies that are slow, flaky, or hard to control, but if the mocking is so extensive that almost none of the function's OWN logic remains exercised, the tests verify only that the mocks do what they were configured to do, not that the real system behaves correctly with real dependencies. The “The tests are excellent, since fully isolating…” option treats isolation as an unconditional goal; isolation is a means to reliable, fast tests, not a reason to mock away the logic you're trying to verify. The “Mocking three dependencies in one test file…” option is wrong: Jest supports mocking any number of modules in one file. The “The tests are equivalent to integration tests…” option is backwards: heavy mocking is the opposite of an integration test, which exercises real dependencies.

assessments.prompt: A function under test awaits a dependency that, in production, performs a real async database call. To simulate that dependency's Promise rejecting with an error in a test, which jest.fn() configuration should be used?
options: mockReturnValue(Promise.resolve(new Error('...'))) -- wrapping the error in a resolved Promise.
mockImplementation(() => { throw new Error('...'); }) is the only valid way to simulate an async rejection; mockRejectedValue does not exist as a Jest API.
mockRejectedValue(new Error('...')) -- this configures the mock to return a Promise that rejects with the given error.
mockReturnValue(new Error('...')) -- this hands back the Error object as a resolved value.
assessments.explanation: mockRejectedValue configures the mock to return a Promise that rejects with the given value, which is what an awaiting caller needs for its await to throw and its try/catch (or .catch()) to engage, simulating a real async failure. The “mockReturnValue(new Error('...')) -- this hands back…” option returns the Error object itself as a plain value, not a rejection, so await receives it as an ordinary value and doesn't throw. The “mockImplementation(() => { throw new Error('...'); })…” option is wrong: mockRejectedValue is a standard Jest API for exactly this. The “mockReturnValue(Promise.resolve(new Error('...'))) -- wrapping the error…” option produces a resolved Promise, not a rejected one, so await on it wouldn't throw.

assessments.prompt: A test file calls jest.mock('./db') and then requires userService.js, which itself internally calls require('./db'). Does userService.js's own internal require also resolve to the mocked version, or to the real module?
options: userService.js's internal require resolves to the same mocked version, because jest.mock('./db') replaces that module for every piece of code loaded within the test file's module resolution, including modules required internally by the file under test.

userService.js's internal require always resolves to the real, unmocked module, since jest.mock only affects requires written directly inside the test file itself, so the only way to test userService.js in isolation is to rewrite it so that it accepts the database as an argument.
userService.js would need to explicitly call jest.mock('./db') itself for its own internal require to be affected; the test file's call alone isn't sufficient.
It depends on whether userService.js uses require or import -- only import-based internal dependencies are affected by jest.mock automatically.
assessments.explanation: jest.mock('./db') intercepts every require/import of that module path within the current test file's module graph: not just the line where the test file requires it, but every later require of that path anywhere the test file's requires lead, including inside userService.js. That's what makes it possible to test userService's real logic while faking its internal database dependency, without userService.js knowing it's under test. The “userService.js's internal require always resolves…”, “It depends on whether userService.js uses require…”, and “userService.js would need to explicitly call jest.mock('./db')…” options all describe a narrower scope than jest.mock has, and none matches how module mocking is designed.

assessments.prompt: According to the distinction the testing literature draws (even though Jest's own API blurs it in everyday use), what specifically separates a 'stub' from a 'mock' in the strict sense?
options: A stub can only return primitive values, while a mock can return objects and arrays.

A stub is a fake that simply returns canned data when called, with no assertions made about how it was called; a mock (in the strict sense) is a fake you additionally make assertions against -- such as checking it was called with specific arguments, or a specific number of times.
A stub always throws an error when invoked, while a mock always returns a successful value.
A stub must be created with jest.fn(), while a mock must be created with jest.mock().
assessments.explanation: The distinction is about what you do with the fake afterward: a stub hands back configured data so the code under test can proceed; a strict mock is also the subject of assertions (toHaveBeenCalledWith, toHaveBeenCalledTimes) verifying that the code under test interacted with it as expected. jest.fn() can serve either role depending on whether you assert on its calls. The “A stub can only return primitive values…” option invents a data-type restriction. The “A stub must be created with jest.fn()…” option is wrong: both stubs and mocks are commonly implemented with jest.fn(), while jest.mock() serves another purpose (replacing a whole module). The “A stub always throws an error…” option invents behavior-based categories unrelated to the stub/mock distinction.

assessments.prompt: Explain to a developer new to testing why unit tests should mock dependencies like databases and third-party APIs, and also explain the risk of mocking too much -- use a concrete example to illustrate the risk.
assessments.modelAnswer: Real dependencies like a database or a third-party payment API introduce problems unrelated to whether your code is correct: network calls make a large suite painfully slow, they can fail or behave inconsistently for reasons unrelated to your logic (the service being down, rate limits, network blips), and some operations have side effects you never want on every test run, like charging a card or sending an email. Mocking replaces the dependency with an in-memory stand-in that returns instantly and can simulate any scenario on demand, including edge cases like 'the database returns null' or 'the payment gateway declines the charge' that are awkward or risky to reproduce against the real thing. The nuance is that a mock should replace the dependency, not the logic you're verifying: a good unit test mocks the boundary (say, db.getUser) while running the real function under test (say, getUserDisplayName, with its real branching), so that logic is exercised. The risk appears when mocking goes further. Imagine a checkout test that mocks the payment gateway to always return { status: 'approved' } and the database to always return a valid cart. If every dependency and edge case is mocked away, what's left running might be one line of glue code connecting the mocks, and the suite could report 100% passing without ever verifying that the real gateway's response shape matches what the mock assumed, or that the real database's error behavior is handled. That's false confidence: the tests are green but mostly prove the mocks do what they were told, not that the system works with its real dependencies, which is the gap integration tests, covered next, close by exercising at least one real path through those boundaries.

concepts.title: Integration Testing an HTTP API with supertest
concepts.description: A unit test verifies one function in isolation; an integration test verifies that several real pieces (routing, middleware, request parsing, response formatting) work correctly together. supertest is the standard tool for driving HTTP requests against an Express app in a test without a separately running server process.
learningObjectives: Explain what an integration test verifies that a unit test with mocked dependencies cannot, using a concrete example.
Write a supertest request against an Express app instance and assert on the response's status code, headers, and body.
Explain why supertest doesn't require calling app.listen() or binding to a real port to test an Express app.
Test both a success path and an error/validation path (e.g. a 400 or 404 response) for a given route.
Structure integration tests so a shared, mutable resource (like a test database or an in-memory store) is reset between tests, mirroring the isolation concerns from unit testing.

sections.heading: What Integration Tests Catch That Unit Tests Don't
sections.body:
The mocking concept ended on a limitation: a unit test that mocks a route handler's dependencies proves the handler's logic is correct given assumptions about what those dependencies return. It doesn't prove that Express calls that handler for the right method and path, that a body-parsing middleware is registered before it (so req.body is populated), that an auth middleware blocks an unauthenticated request before it reaches the handler, or that the JSON sent back has the status code and shape a real client would receive. Each of those is a question about how the pieces of the app are wired together, not about any one function's logic, and an **integration test** is designed to close that gap.

For example, a route intended as app.get('/users/:id', handler) but mistyped as app.get('/user/:id', handler) passes every unit test of handler's logic, since handler is correct, while being unreachable by any real client hitting /users/42. Only a test that sends a request through the real Express app and checks the real response catches a routing mistake like this.

sections.heading: supertest: Driving Real HTTP Requests Without a Real Server
Testing Success and Failure Paths
Isolating State Between Integration Tests
sections.body:
The independence concerns from unit testing apply here with higher stakes, because integration tests often touch a real (if test-only) data store rather than a pure in-memory value. If one test creates a user and a later test asserts 'there is exactly one user in the system,' the tests are coupled through shared, persistent state, and that coupling breaks when tests run in a different order, get filtered, or run in parallel (Jest runs separate test files in parallel by default) against the same underlying store.

The practical patterns: use a separate test database (or an in-memory substitute, like an in-memory SQLite database, or a plain in-memory array in a small example app) rather than a production or shared development database; reset that store in a beforeEach so every test starts from a known baseline, as beforeEach reset the in-memory cart array in the unit-testing concept; and avoid asserting on absolute counts or IDs that depend on what other tests inserted first, preferring assertions scoped to the resource a test itself created or fetched. None of this is specific to integration testing. It's the same 'don't let tests share mutable state' discipline, applied to a data layer instead of a plain variable, with a bigger cost when it goes wrong, since a flaky integration suite is often the first thing a team ignores or disables under deadline pressure.

examples.title: Testing a Full Express App with supertest
examples.explanation: app.js exports the Express app object instead of calling app.listen(). This separation (app.js defines routes, a separate entry file like server.js calls app.listen()) is what lets the test import and drive the app through supertest without binding a fixed port. Both tests exercise the real routing (req.params.id parsing), the real find logic, and the real response formatting end to end. Nothing about users.find or res.json is mocked, because the point of the test is to verify that those pieces work together, not to isolate any one of them.

examples.title: Verifying a Body-Parsing Middleware Is Actually Wired Up
examples.explanation: This test would fail with a useful signal if express.json() were removed or registered after the /echo route: req.body inside the handler would be undefined and the response would not match { message: 'hello' }. That's the kind of wiring mistake a unit test of an isolated handler (called directly with a plain object, bypassing the request-parsing pipeline) can't catch, because it never exercises body parsing. .send({ message: 'hello' }) with a plain object serializes it to JSON and sets the Content-Type header, as a real HTTP client sending a JSON payload would.

misconceptions.description: You need to call app.listen(someport) before supertest can send requests to your Express app, just like you would to test it manually with curl or a browser.
misconceptions.clarification: supertest is designed NOT to require a running, listening server: you pass the Express app object to request(app), and supertest spins up an ephemeral server on a random, unused port for each request, then tears it down. That makes supertest fast and safe to run across parallel test files without port conflicts. Calling app.listen() yourself in a test file is unnecessary and works against the pattern most Express apps use for testability, which is exporting the app object separately from the entry-point file that calls listen() for real deployment.

misconceptions.description: If a route's unit tests (with mocked dependencies) all pass, there's no need for a separate integration test of that same route -- that would just be testing the same logic twice.
misconceptions.clarification: A unit test of a handler's logic and an integration test of the same route verify different things. The unit test proves the handler behaves correctly GIVEN assumptions about how it's invoked and what its mocked dependencies return; it says nothing about whether the route is registered at the right path and method, whether the right middleware runs before it in the right order, or whether the real request/response cycle produces the status code and body shape a real client needs. A typo in the registered path would leave every unit test of the handler passing while making the route unreachable in the real app; only an integration test that sends a real request through the real app catches that.
misconceptions.fact: A unit test of a handler's logic and an integration test of the same route verify genuinely different things, not the same thing twice.

exercises.prompt: Given this Express app and test, does the test pass or fail? Explain why, tracing through what the real app does with the request.
hints: req.body is populated only by a body-parsing middleware like express.json(). Is that middleware registered anywhere in app.js?
Without express.json() registered, what value does req.body have inside the /greet handler when a JSON body is sent?
If req.body is undefined, what happens when the handler reads req.body.name?
exercises.expectedAnswer: The test FAILS, not with a mismatched message but because the handler throws. Without express.json() registered, req.body is undefined, so req.body.name throws a TypeError ('Cannot read properties of undefined'), and Express responds with a 500 error instead of the expected 200 with a greeting.
exercises.solutionExplanation: app.js never calls app.use(express.json()), so nothing parses the incoming request's raw body stream into req.body, and req.body stays undefined for every request whatever the client sent. When the /greet handler executes req.body.name, it reads a property off undefined, which throws a TypeError synchronously inside the handler. Express's default response to a synchronously thrown error in a route handler is a 500 Internal Server Error, so response.status is 500 and expect(response.status).toBe(200) fails. This is a wiring bug (a missing middleware registration) that a unit test calling the handler with a plain JS object, bypassing body parsing, would never surface, but that this integration test, which sends a real HTTP request through the real app, catches immediately.

exercises.prompt: This integration test suite is meant to test creating users independently, but the second test fails when run after the first one (though it passes in isolation). Find the bug and fix it so each test is independent of the others.
hints: The in-memory `users` array lives inside app.js and is shared across every request made to that app instance for the whole test file. Does anything reset it between tests?
The first test already added Amy to `users` before the second test runs. When the second test adds Ben and checks the total count, how many users does the array contain?

Rather than asserting an absolute total count (which depends on everything that ran before it), assert something scoped to the user this test created, or add a reset mechanism (a test-only DELETE /users/_reset route, or re-requiring a fresh app module) that runs in beforeEach.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The in-memory `users` array is module-level state inside app.js, and since both tests use the same already-loaded app module, they share that array for the whole test file; nothing resets it between tests. The first test adds Amy, leaving one user; the second adds Ben, making two, but its assertion assumes the array contains only the user it just added, expecting a length of 1 when it's 2. The fix calls jest.resetModules() inside a beforeEach and re-requires './app' for every test. require normally caches a module and returns the same instance, so resetModules makes Jest re-evaluate app.js from scratch, giving each test a new, empty `users` array and making the tests independent of run order, mirroring the beforeEach state reset used for the plain array in the unit-testing concept.

assessments.prompt: Why does supertest let you write `request(app).get('/health')` without ever calling `app.listen()` in the test file?
options: supertest doesn't actually send real HTTP requests -- it calls the route handler function directly in-process, skipping Express's routing and middleware entirely.
supertest requires a real, already-running server on a well-known port, and silently starts one as a background process the first time it's used.

supertest internally starts an ephemeral server on a random available port for the duration of each request and tears it down afterward, so the real Express routing and middleware pipeline runs, without the test needing to manage a fixed port or a long-lived server process.
app.listen() is called automatically the first time the app module is required, before the test file even runs.
assessments.explanation: supertest takes the Express app object and, per request, starts a temporary HTTP server on an OS-assigned free port, sends a real HTTP request to it, captures the response, and shuts the server down. The routing, middleware, and request/response cycle all run for real, without a fixed port or manual server lifecycle. The “supertest doesn't actually send real HTTP requests…” option is wrong: supertest exercises the real HTTP/Express pipeline, which is why it can catch wiring bugs like a missing body-parser or a mistyped route path. The “app.listen() is called automatically the first time…” option is wrong: requiring an Express app module doesn't call listen(), which is why apps export the bare app object separately from the file that calls listen(). The “supertest requires a real, already-running server…” option is wrong: no pre-existing server on a well-known port is involved, and the port is ephemeral and random per request.

assessments.prompt: A route's handler function is fully correct, and every unit test of it (called directly, with mocked dependencies) passes. But the route was accidentally registered as app.post('/usr', handler) instead of the intended app.post('/user', handler). What does a supertest integration test sending a request to POST /user reveal that the unit tests did not?
options: The integration test also passes, since supertest automatically corrects minor typos in route paths before sending a request.
Nothing different -- since the handler's internal logic is correct, both test types would pass identically.
Express throws a compile-time error before any request is even sent, since it validates every registered route path against a dictionary at startup.

The integration test receives a 404, because supertest drives a real HTTP request through the real Express app's actual routing table, exposing the mistyped path -- something the unit tests never exercise, since they call the handler function directly and bypass routing entirely.
assessments.explanation: A unit test that calls the handler as a plain function never touches Express's routing table, so the typo in app.post('/usr', ...) is invisible to it. An integration test sending a request to /user through the real app exercises the routing table, and since no route matches /user (only the mistyped /usr does), Express responds with its default 404, surfacing the bug. The “Nothing different -- since the handler's internal…” option ignores that the two test types exercise different things. The “The integration test also passes, since supertest…” option invents autocorrection that doesn't exist. The “Express throws a compile-time error before any…” option invents a startup validation step Express doesn't perform.

assessments.prompt: In a supertest request, what does calling .send({ name: 'Amy' }) on a POST request actually do, and why does that matter for testing whether a body-parsing middleware like express.json() is correctly wired up in the app?
options: It only works for GET requests; POST requests require .attach() instead to include any body data.

It serializes the plain object to JSON and sets the appropriate Content-Type header, sending a genuine JSON request body over the request -- exactly mirroring what a real client would send, so req.body only ends up correctly populated in the handler if express.json() is actually registered and working in the app.
It requires the object to already be manually JSON.stringify'd before being passed in, or supertest throws a TypeError immediately.
It bypasses HTTP entirely and injects the object directly into req.body, so it doesn't actually exercise whether express.json() is registered at all.
assessments.explanation: .send() with a plain object serializes it to JSON and sets Content-Type, sending a real request body as an actual HTTP client would, so the route handler sees a populated req.body only if the app's own body-parsing middleware runs and works, which is the wiring a unit test calling the handler directly (with a plain object, bypassing parsing) could never verify. The “It bypasses HTTP entirely and injects…” option misdescribes .send() as a shortcut that skips the real mechanism, when the whole point is that it doesn't. The “It requires the object to already…” option is wrong -- .send() accepts a plain object and serializes it for you. The “It only works for GET requests; POST…” option is wrong -- .send() works with POST (and other body-carrying methods); .attach() is for file uploads specifically, a different use case.

assessments.prompt: Two integration tests in one file both hit a route backed by a shared, module-level in-memory array (let users = [] inside app.js). The first test adds a user; the second test asserts the array's total length is exactly 1, but that assertion fails when the tests run in file order. What is the most robust general fix, consistent with this concept's guidance?
options: Reset the underlying shared state before every test (for example, via jest.resetModules() and re-requiring the app fresh, or an equivalent reset mechanism), and prefer assertions scoped to the specific resource a test itself created rather than absolute counts that depend on what other tests already did.
Remove the second test entirely, since asserting on array length is fundamentally incompatible with integration testing.
Replace toHaveLength(1) with toHaveLength(2) so the assertion matches whatever the actual accumulated count happens to be.
Reorder the tests so the length-checking test always runs first, relying on Jest's default file-order execution to keep working indefinitely.
assessments.explanation: The underlying problem is shared, unreset mutable state leaking between tests, the same independence concern as in unit testing, applied to a data layer. The robust fix mirrors the unit-testing discipline of resetting state before every test (here, re-requiring a fresh app module so its in-memory array starts empty) and avoiding assertions that depend on what other tests did first. The “Reorder the tests so the length-checking test…” option treats a fragile ordering dependency as a permanent solution, which breaks once tests are filtered, reordered, or randomized. The “Replace toHaveLength(1) with toHaveLength(2) so the assertion…” option papers over the symptom by hardcoding today's leaked count instead of fixing the coupling. The “Remove the second test entirely, since asserting…” option throws away a legitimate test instead of fixing the state isolation.

assessments.prompt: A teammate says: 'We already have unit tests for every route handler function with all its dependencies mocked -- writing supertest integration tests on top of that is redundant.' Explain what's wrong with this reasoning, with a concrete example of a bug that unit tests would miss but an integration test would catch.
assessments.modelAnswer: Unit tests with mocked dependencies and integration tests verify different layers of correctness, and thorough coverage of one doesn't make the other redundant. A unit test that calls a route handler directly, with mocked dependencies, proves that GIVEN a request shaped a certain way and GIVEN that its dependencies return certain values, the handler's logic produces the right output. It assumes away everything about how the handler is invoked in the real app: whether it's registered at the right URL and HTTP method, whether the middleware meant to run before it (body parsers, auth checks) is registered in the right order, and whether the real request/response cycle, with real headers, status codes, and serialized JSON, comes out the way a real client needs. For example, suppose a route is meant to be app.post('/users', createUserHandler) but someone writes app.post('/user', createUserHandler), a one-character typo. Every unit test of createUserHandler keeps passing, because those tests call it as a plain function and never go near Express's routing table where the typo lives. A real client, or an integration test, sending POST to the correct path /users gets a 404, because no route was registered at that path. Only an integration test that drives a real HTTP request through the real Express app, which is what supertest is for, exercises the routing table and catches this at once. That's why integration tests complement rather than duplicate unit tests: they cover the wiring of pieces that isolated, mocked unit tests are designed to skip over.
